THE ORIGINS OF REGISTER COMPOSITION
IN PREDYNASTIC EGYPTIAN ART

 

Wurtney M. Davis

Lonpon, ONTARIO

‘The compositions and arrangements of predynastic art are widely supposed to be
thaotic,” and the formal ordering of the historic period is often taken to be the major
point of separation between predynastic and early dynastic art. A striet division between
Egypt's dynastic art and the art of its prehistory is thus frequently accepted. The paper
takes issue with this thesis, for it supposes that there is much more of a link between pre-
historic and historic art than is generally believed. Concentrating upon the origins of
the characteristically dynastic system of register composition in predynastie art, the
paper points out that the register system gradually evolved from certain devices and
techniques of the predynastic period. Certain early features of predynastic art, such as
the depiction of reality, the evolution of narrative, the differentiation between locales
in “landscape” art, and the sequence-patterns on vase-paintings, are discussed in order
to show that the art of the predynastic period did indeed possess an order designed to
represent three-dimensional reality on a two-dimensional surface. It is shown that the
register system was in part derived from these early features of art; in particular, that it was
derived from the use of imaginary base-lines and separation of space in narrative re-
presentation and groundlines and seriality in decorative representation. Phases in the
evolution of the register system, such as a period of coincidence of themes, of coalescence,
and of experimentation, are postulated and considered to set out a possible history of

 

 

   

     

the developments.

to a framework of absolute dates.? The reader
will note that in this paper I shall make no at-

term “period of transition” here denotes only a

Register composition divides the artist’s sur-
face—a wall, palette, mace-head, or other similar
surface suitable for representational carving/
painting—into a series of horizontal bands. These
bands are generally known as “registers.” Re-
gisters usually appear one on top of another,
with the divisions reasonably equidistant through-
out the composition. Nevertheless, certain areas
may not be divided into bands for the space of
several registers (commonly observed in repre-
sentations of the king, whose hieratic scale is
such that he occupies a single “register” the space
of two or more normal registers). I shall concen-
trate mainly upon objects which possess no reg-
gister composition as such; only at the end of
this paper will I consider some “pure” examples.
‘The reason for my emphasis is that the register
technique itself was but the product of the ap-
pearance, growth, and coalescence of a number of
quite different themes in predynastic art! It
must be said, then, that these themes consti-
tute my true interest.

405

Those objects which were later to become the
masterpieces of predynastic art, the most obvious
example being the cosmetic palette, were original-
ly designed for a purely functional purpose. The
earliest palettes—rhomboid slate palettes*—were
clearly utilitarian, and even the more elaborate
theriomorphic palettes were most certainly created
primarily for practical use and only secondarily
for personal ornamentation and the pleasure to be
gained from an aesthetically appealing form, Some
show signs of heavy wear,’ a fact which admonishes
us to rid ourselves of any view of these objects
as priceless objets d'art.

If it is at all necessary to classify the early
palettes as examples of an art-form, they should
be called sculptural. The palettes do not bear a
decoration but are in themselves a decorative or
even a representational form. It is usual for these
sculptural forms to assume the shape of an animal.
Such theriomorphic palettes may in some cases be
derived from the early rhomboid shapes, and
others show a typological relationship with the
later votive palette form in the presence of a
slightly flattened top. Later came incised palettes,
which added simple incised detail to the outline
sculpture of the older theriomorphie variety. Some
incised palettes, for instance, bear notches and
carved-out sections elaborating the sculptural ef-
fect. The development of the palette form, un-
fortunately, is difficult to establish firmly, for
complicating the matter are incised palettes im-
mediately descended from the early “pure” rhom-
boid form without an intervening theriomorphic
stage. And, of course, as the craft developed the
palettes became much more elaborate; some, for
example, were decorated with insets, and others
received decoration in low relief.

Groupings of figures first appeared on incised
palettes.” It seems, however, that we should not

decorative art shifted toward a concern for the
presentation of a “reality,” that is, the representa-
tion of a particular event, and/or space, and/or
time. The artist could not, of course, offer photo-
graphic reproductions of material (physical) real-
ity; he could, however, offer a “rectification of
appearances”® suited to his style without perspec-
tive. I shall speak of the “reality” presented in
predynastic art; I do not suggest, nevertheless,
that art aimed toward precise photographic
naturalism or realism, but rather toward the
presentation of a meaningful, distinctively Egyp-
tian vision of such a reality. Apparently this
was a feature of Egyptian art throughout its
long history.? My use of the term “reality,” then,
is always implicitly qualified. In my view, the
actual presentation of a reality was the first step
toward an ordering of figures in representational
art, of which the register system was later to be
a chief device. Consider some examples.

A Gerzean decorated vase from Abydos" bears
an interesting motif consisting of a bird or birds
in a tree, a kudu, and two long-horned sheep.

Clearer instances of a differentiation between
separate areas or locales are not difficult to dis-
cover on Gerzean pot representations. Another
vase decoration, for example, shows boats, pecu-

(with attendants?), gazelle-like creatures, and
what Capart takes to be summary representations
of ostriches. Here, in the words of one analyst,
the human figures seem to be “floating above”
the boats." Nevertheless, a more consistent pat-
tern emerges if the figures are understood as
either in the boats or as positioned on a shore.
Most likely they are meant to be lining a shore,
for another vase shows the figures noted on the
two pots above definitely outside the boats and
other, anthropoid figures with feet touching the
boats (are they “in” the boats?).5 In general,
on all pots bearing representations of women in

of positioning locales—a sequence, indeed, of a
quite logical nature. ‘The representation progresses
from the water (indicated by boats), up a level
to the shore (women), and up a level again to the
desert’s edge (trees, ostriches) and beyond

I think it highly possible that on some pottery
ware}® artists tried to picture an event, and

perhaps even indicated a space in which the event
was meant to be taking place. However, although
sequences of decoration picture figures occupying
a space, no recognizable attempts were made to
specify an actual place or locality (this is not
surprising: precise identification of region was
rarely made outside of some 19th Dynasty temple
reliefs). We cannot identify more than a very
general landscape on the evidence of the pottery
paintings alone. The reality of these early re-
presentations was a very vague one. It would
seem, too, that the technical as opposed to purely
aesthetic reasons for the practice of sequence
separation are important. As quasi-narrative, these
paintings present a complicated perception of ac-
tuality that has been broken into a group of
smaller, artistically more manageable sections. (It
will not be forgotten that artists were working
without the benefit of perspective). The small
units were then placed at different levels on the
entire surface and ordered so that a consistent
relationship with the original view was maintained.

‘The practice of isolating various elements of a
complex view and thereby simplifying the view
may be termed “separation of space.” Its use is
not limited only to the vases which possess se-
quence-patterns or at least differentiate between
locales, for it also appears in other contexts.
On one pot, which bears a representation of a
human figure with four creatures on a leash,” the
leashed animals and the human figure seem to
occupy completely different planes, although
animals and hunter are supposed to be facing
each other. The perspective rendition of the real
view—what was supposed to be shown—was
beyond predynastic ability, so instead the artist
has broken up this single, complex perspective
view into separate sections. ‘The separate sections
were suited to a non-perspective style with which
the artist could indeed work successfully (see
fig. 3). Note, however, that the relative positions
of the figures have not been unrecognizably al-
tered, Each figure possesses an imaginary base-
line! In one sense, the relative positions of these
imaginary base-lines have not been changed in
the transition from the artist’s actual (perspective)
sighting to his (non-perspective) rendition. If
viewed from above—that is, from an aerial van-
tage-point—the imaginary baselines serve the pur-
pose of indicating and fixing the relative orienta-
tions of the figures. The only thing that has been
altered to fit a style without perspective is the
relationship of each individual figure to its own
imaginary base-line.

My discussion of separation of space anticipates
matter reserved for future comment. What is
important now is that at one point the predynastic
artists began interpretatively to represent some
sort of a reality. Events are portrayed, and we
may postulate a model or actual perspective view
for the representations. And, not least significant-
ly, we may observe fashions of ordering the re-
presentations too artful or too precise to be mere
decoration. It seems that once the initial step
toward depicting a reality was made, a natural
desire to order representations upon the surface
then appeared in sequence-patterns and separa-
tion of space. Let us consider the question of
ordering in more detail.

In the Gerzean period, the decoration of cos-
metic palettes apparently emerged as a distinct
art-form. The advent of figure groupings fitted to
the artifact’s surface in some incised palettes,
and the appearance of low relief carving on con-
temporaneous theriomorphic palettes,*® most prob-
ably created a separate genre with its own canons
and formulae. One of the earliest examples of a
carved palette deserving a note in the history of
art as such is the so-called “Oxford Palette” or
“Small Hierakonpolis Palette.”® The palette is

All of the figures are individually positioned in
a space, for in addition to the imaginary base-line
upon which each is “standing,” all are engaged in
actions suggesting a surrounding space. ‘The over-
all arrangement—that is, the relationships between
figures—is all that confuses us. It seems to me
that the best way to understand what is hap-

will bridge the gulf between a perspective and
a non-perspective sighting. Here I think that we
must turn to the orientations of the imaginary
individual base-lines on the palette for a clue to
the real perspective view which the artist rendered
according to the limits of his ability (see fig. 4).

The application of rows once characteristic of
non-narrative material to narrative representation
is a new development. On the Hunter's Palette,
the old and the new are mixed together, and I
suppose then that the use of the new on the same
object as the old is purely experimental. The
Gebel el Arak handle is experimental in another
sense. In dynastic art, rows or registers present
figures usually separated from each other; in pre-
dynastic examples, a slight degree of overlap
between figures and rows is admitted (here, between
the men’s feet, animals’ legs, and boats’ prows).
On the Gebel el Tarif handle, representations of
carnivores with their paws on other creatures
similarly allows overlap. The row arrangement
on the Gebel el Tarif handle would possess a
vertical precision and “cleanness” if it were not
for intruding decorative rosettes—and why were
the rosettes used in a work with an otherwise
precise serial hierarchy? Decorative motifs were
used earlier to fill in blank spaces surrounding
the major surface interruptions of the object—a
boss, eye-paint saucer, and so on—but on the
Gebel el Tarif handle no such interruption is
found on the side in question. However, it is
likely that the rosettes were employed here for
the same reason as before, that is, to fill in un-
sightly areas of blank space. The row arrange-
ment was clearly not firmly fixed: the artist
apparently felt uncomfortable with a structure
which easily left him with bands of dead space.

Row arrangements and other new usages derived
from a coincidence of once-discrete themes, and
we may observe what may be called an experi-
mental phase in the development of new combined
themes. Now, although I dislike to admit absolute
dates for a late predynastic period, there exist
some objects which are in a typological sense only.
more advanced than late Gerzean experimental
work but which cannot in all cases be dated to the
1st Dynasty. Among their number we must in-
clude the first pure instances of register composi-
tion. Naturally, serial representation (important
because of its great contribution to row arrange-
ments), the use of groundline, and the union of
decorative and narrative devices persisted into
this hypothetical late predynastic period. How-
ever, groundlines now appear on almost all serial
work, whereas before they did not appear on some
varieties of carving, such as the Davis comb and
the Metropolitan and Pitt-Rivers knife handles.

Davis: Register Composition in Predynastic Egyptian Art

On some carved ivories from Hierakonpolis placed
in the transitional period, for instance, ground-
Iines (sometimes carved rather heavily) appear
on definite serial compositions. And true to a
pattern in which the themes of predynastie art
became increasingly more ornate until a change
occurred, the use of groundlines became more
ornate until groundlines as such no longer existed
but were replaced by thick bands of ornamenta-
tion.

Serial arrangements, the various uses of ground-
line and imaginary base-lines, and the use of
separation of space to render clearly a complex
view led to the introduction first of row arrange-
ment in narrative representation, then to the
use of groundlines in decorative serial representa-
tion, and finally to a joint use of row arrange-
ments and groundlines in true register compo-
sition. The first phase of true register composition
continued the tradition of employing artistic de-
vices to separate and clarify a single view or
series of views, and may indeed be said to be but
a more sophisticated instance of the so-called
“chaotic” predynastic separation of space.

On a Hierakonpolitan mace-head,* for example,
a serial arrangement with dividing lines is used in
a single narrative or theme of captives being led
away. Although the composition contains three

One final point that emerges from my analysis
is that there appears to be much more of a link
between quite early predynastic Egyptian art and
dynastic Egyptian art than is often supposed.
Register composition and the earlier separation of
space and its attendant devices were designed
for the same reasons, and the former did not
supersede the latter but rather evolved from it.
